To fasten something means to fix it firmly in place, close it securely, or join it to something else so that it stays put and doesn't move, come apart, or open on its own.

The key feeling behind "fasten" is security and firmness. When you fasten something, you are making sure it won't slip, fall, loosen, or open by itself. There is a deliberate, intentional act involved — you are actively making something stable and secure.
The three main ways "fasten" is used

1. To close or do up something that has a locking or joining mechanism

This is the most everyday use. Many objects around you are designed to be closed or secured using a mechanism — a buckle, a button, a zipper, a latch, a bolt, a clip, a hook. When you use that mechanism to close or secure the object, you are fastening it.

Examples:

  • Fasten your seatbelt before the car moves. (You click the buckle shut so it holds you in place.)
  • She fastened the buttons on her coat one by one.
  • He fastened the zipper on his bag and picked it up.
  • Fasten the lid on the box so nothing falls out.
  • The sailor fastened the ropes tightly before the storm hit.

The opposite action — undoing or opening these things — is called unfastening.

2. To attach or fix one thing to another thing

Here, you are joining or securing one thing onto or to another thing, so that it stays attached and doesn't fall off or separate.

Examples:

  • He fastened the notice to the wall with a pin.
  • She fastened the two pieces of paper together with a paperclip.
  • The workers fastened the wooden planks to the frame with nails.
  • Fasten the badge onto your shirt before the event.

In this use, "fasten" is about creating a connection between two things — and that connection is firm and intended to last, at least for a while.

3. To direct or fix your eyes, mind, or attention firmly on something (figurative)

"Fasten" can also be used in a non-physical, figurative sense. Just as you physically secure something so it doesn't move, you can mentally or visually "fix" your attention, gaze, or thoughts onto something so firmly that it doesn't wander away.

Examples:

  • The child fastened her eyes on the magician and didn't look away.
  • He fastened his attention on every word she said.
  • The audience's gaze was fastened on the stage.

Think of it as: your attention is "locked onto" something, the same way a seatbelt locks into place.

4. To fix blame, guilt, or a label onto someone (figurative)

In this use, "fasten" means to assign or attach something — usually negative, like blame or responsibility — firmly onto a person, in a way that is hard to remove.

Examples:

  • The press fastened the blame on the manager.
  • People were quick to fasten a bad reputation on him.

Here again, the idea of something being stuck firmly carries over from the physical meaning.
How something "fastens" on its own (describing design)

Sometimes, instead of you fastening an object, the object itself is described as fastening in a particular way. This describes how the object is designed to close or be secured.

Examples:

  • This dress fastens at the back. (Meaning: its closure mechanism — buttons, zip, or hooks — is located at the back.)
  • The bag fastens with a magnetic clip.
  • The jacket fastens with velcro.
The feeling and emphasis that "fasten" carries

What separates "fasten" from just saying "close" or "attach" is the sense of security and firmness it implies.

  • If you say you closed a box, it just means the lid is down.
  • If you say you fastened a box, it means the lid is secured — it's not going to flip open.

Similarly:

  • Attaching something can be loose or temporary.
  • Fastening something suggests it is held firmly and reliably.

"Fasten" also implies intentionality — you make a conscious decision and physical effort to secure something. It is never accidental.
How "fasten" is different from similar words

Similar wordHow it differs from "fasten"

Fix — "Fix" often means to repair something. It can also mean to hold something in place, but "fasten" is more specific about the act of securing using a mechanism or connection.

Secure — Very close in meaning to "fasten" and often interchangeable, but "secure" tends to sound more formal or serious (you secure a building; you fasten your seatbelt).

Tie — A specific way of fastening, using rope, string, or laces. All tying is fastening, but not all fastening is tying.

Button / Zip / Buckle / Latch — These are all specific ways of fastening. "Fasten" is the broader word that covers all of them.

Attach — More neutral and general; it doesn't carry the same emphasis on firmness and security that "fasten" does.
Common and natural ways "fasten" is used in everyday life

• Fasten your seatbelt — the instruction you hear on every flight and in every car.
  • Fasten the door — lock or bolt the door securely.
  • Fasten a knot — tie and tighten it so it holds.
  • Fasten a hook — clip or latch a hook into place.
  • Fasten two ends together — join them so they don't come apart.
A simple way to remember it

Whenever you see or hear "fasten," picture a seatbelt clicking firmly into place. That single image captures everything: the intentional action, the mechanism, the firmness, the security, and the fact that it is designed not to come undone on its own. That is what "fasten" means — in almost any context you will ever encounter it.
